tagline: Israel's busiest port, built on the dunes from 1956
lines: Modern Ashdod was approved on 1 May 1956; its first 22 families came from Morocco.
Ashdod's port is Israel's largest and handles about 60% of the country's imports.
Port works began in 1961 and the first ships were worked there in 1965.
Ashdod was planned in numbered quarters of 10,000 to 15,000 people each.
About 228,000 people live here, making it Israel's sixth-largest city.
Ashdod has the world's largest Georgian Jewish community.
Over 100,000 newcomers arrived between 1990 and 2001, mostly from the former USSR.
Ancient Ashdod was one of the five Philistine cities, named 13 times in the Bible.
The Museum of Philistine Culture calls itself the only one of its kind in the world.
The art museum's entrance is a glass pyramid in the cultural district.
The Ashdod Yam fortress by the sea is a medieval ruin, restored in 2020.
Givat Yona, Jonah's Hill, is the city's highest point and has a lighthouse.
A sand dune reserve runs about 20 km along the city's southern edge.
The coast here is about 8 km long, with a string of public beaches.
known_for: The marina and Ashdod Yam fortress
Immigrant communities from Morocco, Georgia and the former USSR
history: 17th c. BCE: a fortified Canaanite town rises at Tel Ashdod
Iron Age: one of the five Philistine city-states
1948: the Arab town of Isdud is depopulated in the war
1956: modern Ashdod founded on the coastal dunes
1958: the Eshkol power station is completed
1965: the new port handles its first cargo
1990s: a big wave of immigrants from the former Soviet Union

neighbourhoods.name: Port and northern industry
neighbourhoods.mood: Cranes, containers and the power station, cut off by the Lachish stream

neighbourhoods.name: Rova HaKirya (the City)
neighbourhoods.mood: The busiest quarter: city hall, City mall and bus station, Herzl and Begin

neighbourhoods.name: Marina quarter
neighbourhoods.mood: Newer towers by about 550 yacht berths and the Ashdod Yam park

neighbourhoods.name: Rova Alef (Quarter A)
neighbourhoods.mood: The old centre: Rogozin pedestrian street, Ashdod Mall, near Kashtot beach

neighbourhoods.name: Rova Bet (Quarter B)
neighbourhoods.mood: The daily open market and Ben-Gurion Park

neighbourhoods.name: Rova Dalet (Quarter D)
neighbourhoods.mood: The Philistine museum and a Samson statue on Moshe Dayan boulevard

neighbourhoods.name: Rova Gimel (Quarter G)
neighbourhoods.mood: A long-standing religious quarter, home to the Grodno Yeshiva

neighbourhoods.name: Rova Yud-Gimel (Quarter 13)
neighbourhoods.mood: Streets named for the kings of Judah and Israel around a central park

neighbourhoods.name: Rova Tet-Vav (Quarter 15)
neighbourhoods.mood: The southern end, near Rothschild park and the Riviera beach

streets.Sderot Bnei Brit: Named for B'nai B'rith, the Jewish service group; a newer bus terminal carries its name
streets.Sderot Moshe Dayan: Honours the general and defence minister; runs parallel to the sea, home of the city run
streets.Sderot Herzl: Honours Theodor Herzl, founder of political Zionism; a main road through the City quarter
streets.Menachem Begin: Honours the prime minister; its tunnel passes under Ilan Ramon Square in the City
streets.Sderot Altalena: Named for the Altalena, the arms ship sunk off Tel Aviv in a June 1948 clash
streets.Sderot Ben Ami: Honours Oved Ben-Ami, who co-founded the company that built Ashdod
streets.Sderot Jerusalem: Named for Israel's capital; one of the city's main boulevards
streets.Sderot Moshe Sne: Honours Moshe Sne, a pre-state Haganah commander and later politician
streets.Sderot Yitzhak Rabin: Honours the prime minister assassinated in 1995
streets.Jabotinsky: Honours Ze'ev Jabotinsky, Revisionist Zionist leader; it has bus-priority lanes
streets.HaNeft: Means 'the oil' in Hebrew, an industrial-sounding name

food: Beachfront restaurants and bars at Kashtot (Gandhi) beach
Cheap street snacks from about 15 shekels
The daily municipal open market in Quarter B
A Wednesday farmers and clothes market near Lido beach
Moroccan and Georgian home cooking from the city's big communities
rhythm: Weekdays the port, industrial zones and the City quarter around Herzl and Begin fill with traffic and buses. Friday afternoon things wind down for Shabbat, which is quiet, especially in the large Haredi quarters (the musical fountain doesn't run on Friday nights). Evenings and summer weekends draw people to the beaches, the promenade and the marina.
